newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia car shares seen outdoing market-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia car shares seen outdoing market-analysts.

text.p: Shares of Malaysia's car makers and distributors are likely to outperform the local stock market this year, driven by strong economic growth and protection for the local car, analysts said on Wednesday.
"Grossly undervalued, overweight," was Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's recommendation on the sector in a recent report.
Passenger car sales in April 1997 rose to 24,582 units, compared to 24,189 units in April 1996, said the Malaysian Motor Traders Association on Wednesday.
Sales for the first quarter of 1997 grew by around 11 percent over the same period in 1996.
"Another year of stellar earnings growth (29 percent) in 1997 is almost in hand for auto groups. Vehicle sales have remained robust, albeit growing at an easier pace," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

The benchmark Kuala Lumpur Composite Index, a weighted average of 100 large-capitalised blue-chip stocks, rose by around 24 percent in 1996. But since January 1997, the index has dropped nine percent.

"More importantly, most of the growth is in commercial four-wheel-drive vehicles which are usually exposed to the 'productive' revenue-generating activities of the economy," the Deutsche Morgan Grenfell report said.
Analysts' main reasons to be cheerful about the sector are based on strong economic growth, and changing demographic trends.

"We are overweight on the sector. Motor sales are good, there were concerns over the yen's strength last year, but it is now down on last year," said Choo Swee Kee, automotive analyst at Vickers Ballas.
The Japanese currency has depreciated around 16 percent against the ringgit over the year to March 31, 1997.
The main players in Malaysia's auto sector include national car maker Perusahaan Otomobil Nasional Bhd (Proton) and distributor Edaran Otomobil Nasional (EON).
The auto group is also made up of UMW Holdings Bhd, Tan Chong Motor Holdings Bhd, and Oriental Holdings Bhd, which respectively assemble and distribute Toyota, Nissan and Honda vehicles.
With around 60 percent of Proton's component costs denominated in yen, and Malaysia's high demand for Japanese cars, the sector is vulnerable to fluctuations in the ringgit/yen exchange rate.
In addition, companies like MBM Resources Bhd and Sapura Motors Bhd make and supply parts, mainly for Proton.

"Malaysia has a very young population who like to replace their cars frequently, and demographic trends show the number of people per household dropping, which also means they would want to have their own cars. Of course, the economy helps a lot," said an automotive analyst at a foreign brokerage house in Kuala Lumpur.
But the peaking of the current replacement cycle in 1996, and the possibility of a rebound in the value of the yen "reduces the upside for the sector as a whole", said the analyst.
"I'm overweight on the sector on a three-month basis, but neutral looking ahead 12 months," he said.
